title: Leveling the Playing Field -- Ch. 20: Romualdez v. Sandiganbayan: Constitutionality of the Anti-Graft Law
keywords: Section 17 of Article VII of the 1973 Constitution
primary_topics: Chapter 20 of 'Leveling the Playing Field' -- CJP's account of Romualdez v. Sandiganbayan, the case that gave the Court the chance to close the debate left open by Estrada v. Sandiganbayan on whether the void-for-vagueness doctrine may be used to strike down penal laws

The Court's holding that the overbreadth and vagueness doctrines have special application only to free-speech cases, so that Section 5 of Republic Act 3019 -- directed at conduct, not speech -- could be tested only 'as applied' to Romualdez

The procedural ground that would alone have justified dismissal: Romualdez's repetitive motions to quash and dismiss, since the Rules abhor repetitive motions and a party may not raise issues by installment

The disposal of his remaining claims -- a vague Information, a defective preliminary investigation, prescription, and derivative executive immunity -- and Justice Tinga's Separate Opinion insisting that a vagueness challenge to a penal law is a proper invocation of due process
sub_topics: The unfinished business from Estrada v. Sandiganbayan: the Court upheld the Anti-Plunder Law but did not meet head on the 'on its face' vagueness and overbreadth challenge, merely citing Justice Vicente V. Mendoza's Separate Concurring Opinion that the doctrines apply only to free speech

The line-up in Estrada -- Bellosillo's ponencia and Mendoza's opinion joined by Davide, Melo, Puno, Vitug and Quisumbing, with CJP writing a Separate Concurring Opinion, Kapunan, Pardo, Santiago and Gutierrez dissenting, and Carpio taking no part -- and the 10-4-1 vote that left constitutionalists still debating
The facts: Alfredo T. Romualdez, brother-in-law of former President Marcos, was charged by the PCGG on July 12, 1989 with violating Section 5 of RA 3019

His litigation history: a 1996 Motion to Dismiss and to Defer Arraignment, a Sandiganbayan order to seek reinvestigation, a failed 1998 certiorari petition, a Motion to Quash recommended for dismissal by the Special Prosecutor but overruled by Ombudsman Desierto, a second Motion to Quash in 1999, and a third Motion to Dismiss admitted in 2001

The Sandiganbayan's rulings: the immunity provision of the 1973 Constitution took effect only in 1981 and could not cover a 1975 offense; his right to preliminary investigation was satisfied by reinvestigation; and the Information set forth the essential elements
The five issues before the Supreme Court: constitutionality of Section 5, vagueness of the Information, validity of the preliminary investigation, prescription, and immunity from prosecution

Repetitive motions prohibited: the supplemental motion was in effect a third motion to quash, there is no substantial distinction between a motion to quash and a motion to dismiss, and the Petition deserved outright dismissal -- but the Court reached the merits given the importance of the case in curtailing graft and corruption
Constitutionality: statutes are presumed valid and the challenger carries the onerous burden of rebutting that presumption, which Romualdez miserably failed to do

The Dans v. People test -- a penal law is not vague if it adequately answers 'What is the violation?' -- satisfied by the two elements of Section 5: the offender's relationship within the third civil degree to named officials, and his direct or indirect intervention in a government business, transaction, contract or application

The word 'intervene' is not indefinite: the absence of a statutory definition does not render a law void for vagueness where construction supplies the ordinary meaning, 'to come between,' with the details of intervention left to trial
Vague Information: the remedy is a motion for a bill of particulars, not a motion to quash, and the Information here described the offense with enough particularity for an intelligent defense

Preliminary investigation: although the PCGG could not investigate a complaint it had initiated (Cojuangco v. PCGG), the Sandiganbayan had suspended trial and afforded reinvestigation by the Ombudsman, consistent also with Raro v. Sandiganbayan

Prescription: Act No. 3326 governs offenses under special laws, and for pre-1986 RA 3019 cases the period runs from discovery -- here after the PCGG's investigations, making the July 12, 1989 Information timely

Immunity: the 1981 amendment could not cover a 1975 act, and under Estrada v. Desierto executive immunity attaches only during a President's incumbency, so no derivative immunity could pass to a naval aide-de-camp

Justice Tinga's Separate Opinion: the Estrada pronouncement on vagueness was obiter, not ratio; the Bill of Rights holds primacy; a statute whose standards leave men of common intelligence guessing violates due process; and a mode of challenge open to one deprived of property should be more available to one in jeopardy of liberty or life
CJP's closing inference that the 'in the result' votes of Justices Puno, Santiago and Gutierrez signaled their own reservations about the void-for-vagueness discussion
signature_phrases: Given the importance of the case in curtailing graft and corruption
the over-breadth and the vagueness doctrines had special application only to free-speech cases

stances.claim: The overbreadth and void-for-vagueness doctrines have special application only to free-speech cases and are not appropriate for testing penal statutes; because Section 5 of RA 3019 targets conduct rather than speech, it could be examined only as applied to the accused and not struck down on its face.
stances.rhetorical_move: doctrinal confinement, completing the analysis Estrada had left to a separate opinion and settling it as a holding

stances.claim: A penal provision is not vague when it adequately answers the question 'What is the violation?'; the absence of a statutory definition of a term such as 'intervene' does not void a law, since construction supplies its ordinary meaning, and the hows and whys are evidentiary matters for trial.
stances.rhetorical_move: applying a settled test from Dans v. People and resolving the word by ordinary statutory construction

stances.claim: Romualdez's serial motions were procedurally fatal -- a motion to dismiss was in substance a prohibited second motion to quash, the Rules abhor repetitive motions, and issues may not be raised by installment -- so the Petition deserved outright dismissal even before its merits were reached.
stances.rhetorical_move: procedural rebuke first, then a deliberate decision to address the merits anyway because of the case's importance in curtailing graft

stances.claim: Justice Tinga argued that Estrada's pronouncement on vagueness was obiter rather than ratio, and that a vagueness challenge to a penal statute is a proper invocation of the due process clause, which must be at least as available to one in jeopardy of liberty or life as to one deprived of property.
stances.rhetorical_move: faithful reproduction of a colleague's counterargument, set out at length before CJP's closing inference about the 'in the result' votes

notable_anecdotes: CJP recalls that he wrote a Separate Concurring Opinion in Estrada v. Sandiganbayan, and that Justice Carpio took no part there because he had been one of the complainants against Estrada before the Ombudsman.

He notes that even after the 10-4-1 vote in Estrada, some constitutionalists still argued the on-its-face challenge remained open because the ponencia had merely cited the Mendoza opinion rather than confronting the issue.

He traces Romualdez's long procedural campaign -- three motions to dismiss or quash, a failed certiorari petition, and a Special Prosecutor's recommendation to dismiss that Ombudsman Desierto overruled -- as the backdrop to the Court's impatience with repetitive motions.

He explains that no one before February 1986 would have dared question the transaction, so that the offense was discovered only through the PCGG's exhaustive investigations, making the 1989 Information timely.

He closes with a personal inference: since Justices Santiago and Gutierrez had dissented in Estrada, he surmises that their 'in the result' votes here reflected a continuing reservation about the void-for-vagueness holding.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 20 of 'Leveling the Playing Field' recounted how Romualdez v. Sandiganbayan gave the Supreme Court the occasion to settle a question that Estrada v. Sandiganbayan had left open: whether the void-for-vagueness doctrine may be used to invalidate penal laws. In Estrada the Court had upheld the Anti-Plunder Law by a 10-4-1 vote but had not met the 'on its face' challenge head on, merely citing Justice Mendoza's Separate Concurring Opinion that overbreadth and vagueness apply only to free-speech cases; CJP himself had written a Separate Concurring Opinion there. Romualdez, a brother-in-law of former President Marcos charged by the PCGG in 1989 with violating Section 5 of Republic Act 3019, attacked that provision as vague and overbroad after a long train of motions to dismiss and to quash. The Court first held those motions procedurally fatal -- a motion to dismiss was in substance a prohibited second motion to quash, the Rules abhor repetitive motions, and issues may not be raised by installment -- yet reached the merits because of the importance of the case in curtailing graft and corruption. It then held that the doctrines have special application only to free-speech cases, that a statute aimed at conduct is tested only as applied, that every statute is presumed valid, and that under Dans v. People the law adequately answered 'What is the violation?' through its two elements; the word 'intervene' meant simply 'to come between.' A vague Information called for a bill of particulars, not a quashal; the reinvestigation by the Ombudsman satisfied Cojuangco and Raro; prescription ran from discovery after the PCGG's work, so the 1989 Information was timely; and immunity failed because the 1981 amendment could not reach a 1975 act and, under Estrada v. Desierto, immunity attaches only during incumbency. CJP closed by reproducing Justice Tinga's Separate Opinion that the Estrada pronouncement was obiter and that a vagueness challenge is a proper due process claim.
